title: Teaming up with Frankie Laine
summary: Marsala lets Frankie Laine sing, and Hodes and Laine join forces for small jobs like Passaic, New Jersey. Hodes describes Laine's early swinging style and charm with bookers.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: So here I am, out of work. I'm too nervous to keep that job. I played that night, but I played with my head turned, watching the window and all that. It just wasn't worth it. And so I thanked Joe for the chance, and he told me to keep coming in. And it was there that Frankie Laine was singing. He was down on his ass, so to speak, and Joe was just kind enough to hand him a chance for, like, say, five dollars.

He was from Cleveland. But he'd been -- I didn't think he needed Frankie Laine at all. But Joe was that kind of kind person. He just -- he needs the air time, give him a break. And so he let him sing. And that's where we met. I'd come in there a couple of times, and he'd sing and I'd play. We were both out or work, so he thought it was -- I might be getting a little ahead, but I'd like to get this part, because he thought it would be a good idea that two can do better what one can't seem to do. Let's join forces.

So we became a team called Laine and Hodes, which always irritated me at that time because I thought it should be Hodes and Laine. In fact, when we got the team up to the point where we'd make $50 a week apiece, it became too much for us.

This was in New York between the years of 1938 and about '40. And we did work. We took jobs in Passaic, New Jersey, and we took a five dollar apiece job to sing for one night or something. We did anything to work. And we did find some work, because Frankie was the kind of guy that would charm the office girl. And he'd say to me, don't you go up there, let me go up there, I'll charm her. And he'd get to see the manager or the booking office man. And so that's what he would do and turn around, and -- but he was always good to me. The only bone of contention was that. I like the way

he sang. I wasn't ecstatic about it but I liked the way he sang, because he swung. He could swing. And at that time, it's not the Frankie Laine you hear now, he didn't have the same thing. Everything was off the cuff. Sing two choruses and the piano would take one, and sing another one.
And you hadn't known him in Chicago.
